# @isaacs/ttlcache

The time-based use-recency-unaware cousin of
[`lru-cache`](http://npm.im/lru-cache)

## Usage

Essentially, this is the same API as
[`lru-cache`](http://npm.im/lru-cache), but it does not do LRU tracking,
and is bound primarily by time, rather than space. Since entries are not
purged based on recency of use, it can save a lot of extra work managing
linked lists, mapping keys to pointers, and so on.

TTLs are millisecond granularity.

If a capacity limit is set, then the soonest-expiring items are purged
first, to bring it down to the size limit.

Iteration is in order from soonest expiring until latest expiring.

If multiple items are expiring in the same ms, then the soonest-added
items are considered "older" for purposes of iterating and purging down to
capacity.

A TTL _must_ be set for every entry, which can be defaulted in the
constructor.

Custom size calculation is not supported. Max capacity is simply the count
of items in the cache.

```js
import { TTLCache } from '@isaacs/ttlcache'
const cache = new TTLCache({ max: 10000, ttl: 1000 })

// set some value
cache.set(1, 2)

// 999 ms later
cache.has(1) // returns true
cache.get(1) // returns 2

// 1000 ms later
cache.get(1) // returns undefined
cache.has(1) // returns false
```

## Caveat Regarding Timers and Graceful Exits

On Node.js, this module uses the `Timeout.unref()` method to
prevent its internal `setTimeout` calls from keeping the process
running indefinitely. However, on other systems such as Deno,
where the `setTimeout` method does not return an object with an
`unref()` method, the process will stay open as long as any
unexpired entry exists in the cache.

You may call `cache.cancelTimer()` to clear the timeout and
allow the process to exit normally. Be advised that canceling the
timer in this way will of course prevent anything from expiring.

## API

### `const { TTLCache } = require('@isaacs/ttlcache')` or `import { TTLCache } from '@isaacs/ttlcache'`

The `TTLCache` class is a named export.

### `new TTLCache({ ttl, max = Infinty, updateAgeOnGet = false, checkAgeOnGet = false, noUpdateTTL = false, noDisposeOnSet = false })`

Create a new `TTLCache` object.

- `max` The max number of items to keep in the cache. Must be
  positive integer or `Infinity`, defaults to `Infinity` (ie,
  limited only by TTL, not by item count).
- `ttl` The max time in ms to store items. Overridable on the `set()`
  method. Must be a positive integer or `Infinity` (see note
  below about immortality hazards). If `undefined` in
  constructor, then a TTL _must_ be provided in each `set()`
  call.
- `updateAgeOnGet` Should the age of an item be updated when it is
  retrieved? Defaults to `false`. Overridable on the `get()` method.
- `checkAgeOnGet` Check the TTL whenever an item is retrieved
  with `get()`. If the item is past its ttl, but the timer has
  not yet fired, then delete it and return undefined. By default,
  the cache will return a value if it has one, even if it is
  technically beyond its TTL.
- `noUpdateTTL` Should setting a new value for an existing key leave the
  TTL unchanged? Defaults to `false`. Overridable on the `set()` method.
  (Note that TTL is _always_ updated if the item is expired, since that is
  treated as a new `set()` and the old item is no longer relevant.)
- `dispose` Method called with `(value, key, reason)` when an item is
  removed from the cache. Called once item is fully removed from cache.
  It is safe to re-add at this point, but note that adding when `reason` is
  `'set'` can result in infinite recursion if `noDisponseOnSet` is not
  specified.

  Disposal reasons:
  - `'stale'` TTL expired.
  - `'set'` Overwritten with a new different value.
  - `'evict'` Removed from the cache to stay within capacity limit.
  - `'delete'` Explicitly deleted with `cache.delete()` or
    `cache.clear()`

- `noDisposeOnSet` Do not call `dispose()` method when overwriting a key
  with a new value. Defaults to `false`. Overridable on `set()` method.

When used as an iterator, like `for (const [key, value] of cache)` or
`[...cache]`, the cache yields the same results as the `entries()` method.

### `cache.size`

The number of items in the cache.

### `cache.set(key, value, { ttl, noUpdateTTL, noDisposeOnSet } = {})`

Store a value in the cache for the specified time.

`ttl` and `noUpdateTTL` optionally override defaults on the constructor.

Returns the cache object.

### `cache.get(key, {updateAgeOnGet, checkAgeOnGet, ttl} = {})`

Get an item stored in the cache. Returns `undefined` if the item is not in
the cache (including if it has expired and been purged).

If `updateAgeOnGet` is `true`, then re-add the item into the
cache with the updated `ttl` value. All options default to the
settings on the constructor.

If `checkAgeOnGet`, then an item will be deleted if it is found
to be beyond its TTL, which can happen if the setTimeout timer
has not yet fired to trigger its expiration.

Note that using `updateAgeOnGet` _can_ effectively simulate a
"least-recently-used" type of algorithm, by repeatedly updating
the TTL of items as they are used. However, if you find yourself
doing this, consider using
[`lru-cache`](http://npm.im/lru-cache), as it is much more
optimized for an LRU use case.

### `cache.getRemainingTTL(key)`

Return the remaining time before an item expires. Returns `0` if the item
is not found in the cache or is already expired.

### `cache.has(key)`

Return true if the item is in the cache.

### `cache.delete(key)`

Remove an item from the cache.

### `cache.clear()`

Delete all items from the cache.

### `cache.entries()`

Return an iterator that walks through each `[key, value]` from soonest
expiring to latest expiring. (Items expiring at the same time are walked
in insertion order.)

Default iteration method for the cache object.

### `cache.keys()`

Return an iterator that walks through each `key` from soonest expiring to
latest expiring.

### `cache.values()`

Return an iterator that walks through each `value` from soonest expiring to
latest expiring.

### `cache.cancelTimer()`

Clear the internal timer, and stop automatically expiring items
when their TTL expires.

This allows the process to exit normally on Deno and other
platforms that lack Node's `Timer.unref()` method.

## Internal Methods

You should not ever call these, they are managed automatically.

### `purgeStale`

**Internal**

Removes items which have expired. Called automatically.

### `purgeToCapacity`

**Internal**

Removes soonest-expiring items when the capacity limit is reached. Called
automatically.

### `dispose`

**Internal**

Called when an item is removed from the cache and should be disposed. Set
this on the constructor options.

### `setTimer`

**Internal**

Called when an item with a ttl is added. This ensures that only one timer
is setup at once. Called automatically.

## Algorithm

The cache uses two `Map` objects. The first maps item keys to their
expiration time, and the second maps item keys to their values. Then, a
null-prototype object uses the expiration time as keys, with the value
being an array of all the keys expiring at that time.

This leverages a few important features of modern JavaScript engines for
fairly good performance:

- `Map` objects are highly optimized for referring to arbitrary values by
  arbitrary keys.
- Objects with solely integer-numeric keys are iterated in sorted numeric
  order rather than insertion order, and insertions in the middle of the
  key ordering are still very fast. This is true of all modern JS engines
  tested at the time of this module's creation, but most particularly V8
  (the engine in Node.js).

When it is time to prune, we can always walk the null-prototype object in
iteration order, deleting items until we come to the first key greater than
the current time.

Thus, the `start` time doesn't need to be tracked, only the expiration
time. When an item age is updated (either explicitly on `get()`, or by
setting to a new value), it is deleted and re-inserted.

## Immortality Hazards

It is possible to set a TTL of `Infinity`, in which case an item
will never expire. As it does not expire, its TTL is not
tracked, and `getRemainingTTL()` will return `Infinity` for that
key.

If you do this, then the item will never be purged. Create
enough immortal values, and the cache will grow to consume all
available memory. If find yourself doing this, it's _probably_
better to use a different data structure, such as a `Map` or
plain old object to store values, as it will have better
performance and the hazards will be more obvious.

...

Tiny async cache: TTL + LRU , single-flight dedup, and stale-while-revalidate . Zero dependencies .
CI npm version bundle size types license
Caching an expensive async call sounds simple — until ten requests for the same cold key arrive at once and all ten hit your database (a cache stampede ), or a value expires mid-traffic and every

...

Concurrent calls for the same key share a single in-flight promise instead of all recomputing.
* No latency cliff. With staleWhileRevalidate , expiry returns the cached value immediately and refreshes in the background — readers never wait on a slow recompute.
* TTL + LRU built in. Per-entry TTL and least-recently-used eviction.
* Failures aren't cached. A rejected computation propagates and is retried next call, not memoized.
* Zero dependencies , ESM + CJS + types, and an injectable clock for tests.

Install

npm install flightcache
# or: pnpm add flightcache  /  yarn add flightcache  /  bun add flightcache

API

memoize(fn, options?) → memoized

Wrap an async (or sync) function. The returned function caches by key and exposes .cache , .invalidate(...args) , and .clear() .
* Option | Type | Default | Description
* ttl | number (ms) | 60000 | How long a value stays fresh.
* staleWhileRevalidate | number (ms) | 0 | Extra window to serve stale while refreshing.
* max | number | unbounded | LRU cap on cached keys.
* key | (...args) => string | JSON.stringify(args) | Derive the cache key from arguments.
* singleFlight | boolean | true | Coalesce concurrent same-key calls.
* clock | () => number | Date.now | Injectable clock for deterministic tests.
const m = memoize(fetchThing, { ttl: 5_000 });
await m("a");
m.invalidate("a"); // drop one key
m.clear();         // drop everything
m.cache.size;      // inspect the underlying cache

TTLCache<K, V>

The storage layer on its own — a TTL + LRU map.
import { TTLCache } from "flightcache";

const cache = new TTLCache<string, Buffer>({ max: 500, ttl: 10_000 });
cache.set("k", buf);
cache.get("k");    // bumps recency; undefined if expired
cache.peek("k");   // no recency change
cache.has("k");
cache.delete("k");
cache.keys();      // live keys, oldest → newest

## Storage Bounds Safety

This implementation aims to be as flexible as possible, within
the limits of safe memory consumption and optimal performance.

At initial object creation, storage is allocated for `max` items.
If `max` is set to zero, then some performance is lost, and item
count is unbounded. Either `maxSize` or `ttl` _must_ be set if
`max` is not specified.

If `maxSize` is set, then this creates a safe limit on the
maximum storage consumed, but without the performance benefits of
pre-allocation. When `maxSize` is set, every item _must_ provide
a size, either via the `sizeCalculation` method provided to the
constructor, or via a `size` or `sizeCalculation` option provided
to `cache.set()`. The size of every item _must_ be a positive
integer.

If neither `max` nor `maxSize` are set, then `ttl` tracking must
be enabled. Note that, even when tracking item `ttl`, items are
_not_ preemptively deleted when they become stale, unless
`ttlAutopurge` is enabled. Instead, they are only purged the
next time the key is requested. Thus, if `ttlAutopurge`, `max`,
and `maxSize` are all not set, then the cache will potentially
grow unbounded.

In this case, a warning is printed to standard error. Future
versions may require the use of `ttlAutopurge` if `max` and
`maxSize` are not specified.

If you truly wish to use a cache that is bound _only_ by TTL
expiration, consider using a `Map` object, and calling
`setTimeout` to delete entries when they expire. It will perform
much better than an LRU cache.

Here is an implementation you may use, under the same
[license](./LICENSE) as this package:

```js
// a storage-unbounded ttl cache that is not an lru-cache
const cache = {
  data: new Map(),
  timers: new Map(),
  set: (k, v, ttl) => {
    if (cache.timers.has(k)) {

// ✅ Recommended for TTL tests
// mocking timers, e.g. jest.useFakeTimers()
const { LRUCache } = await import('lru-cache')
```

This ensures that your mocked timers or time sources are
respected when testing TTL behavior.

Additionally, you can pass in a `perf` option when creating your
LRUCache instance. This option accepts any object with a `now`
method that returns a number.

For example, this would be a very bare-bones time-mocking system
you could use in your tests, without any particular test
framework:

```ts
import { LRUCache } from 'lru-cache'

let myClockTime = 0

const cache = new LRUCache<string>({
  max: 10,
  ttl: 1000,
  perf: {
    now: () => myClockTime,
  },
})

// run tests, updating myClockTime as needed
```

## Breaking Changes in Version 7

This library changed to a different algorithm and internal data
structure in version 7, yielding significantly better
performance, albeit with some subtle changes as a result.

If you were relying on the internals of LRUCache in version 6 or
before, it probably will not work in version 7 and above.

I'm weighing whether to adopt lru-cache for this, since it supports injecting performance and its TTL-only, unbounded setup prints a stderr warning. Its own docs suggest a plain Map for that case, and the user's setup is unbounded with a 30-second TTL, which lru-cache's LRU eviction doesn't really serve. The repo also has no package manifest to add it to.

I'm still weighing the semantics here: the user's "change the TTL to 30 s" points to TTL behavior, and expired entries only get removed when read again, so distinct ids could pile up in memory over time. I'm considering whether a sweep on insert is worth the cost, or whether lazy eviction is enough for this case.

I'm working out the cache's expiry: entries are fixed-TTL and reads don't extend them, so a Map's insertion order matches expiry order and I can prune expired entries from the front on each lookup. For timing, I'm leaning toward Date.now() since bun's setSystemTime can test it, though a clock change could shift lifetimes, which I'll note as a risk.

Date.now is the time source, with the clock-jump risk noted. The gate checks out: no concurrency state, so the standard path applies. Next I'll write the artifacts in the worktree.

# Proposal

## Why

`getWidget(id)` in `src/cache.ts` builds a new widget object on every call, so callers asking for the same id never share a result. Caching each widget for 30 seconds lets repeated lookups reuse one instance while still picking up a fresh widget after a bounded time, and an explicit invalidation API lets callers drop a stale entry before it expires.

## What Changes

- `getWidget(id)` returns the same widget instance for the same id while that id's cache entry is younger than 30 seconds (30 000 ms).
- An entry expires 30 000 ms after it was created; reads do not extend its lifetime. The first lookup after expiry builds a new widget and starts a new 30-second entry.
- New export `invalidateWidget(id)`: drops that id's entry so the next lookup builds a new widget; other ids are unaffected; an id with no entry is a no-op.
- New export `clearWidgetCache()`: drops every entry.
- The returned widget's shape (`{ id }`) and the `getWidget` signature are unchanged.

Decisions taken with the user before this proposal: time-based expiry (30 s TTL, set after the user's correction from an earlier no-expiry choice), no size bound, and an exported invalidation API.

## Capabilities

### New Capabilities
- `widget-lookup`: looking up a widget by id, including how long a looked-up widget is reused and how callers invalidate it.

### Modified Capabilities

None: the repository has no specs (`openspec list --specs` reports none).

## Impact

- Code: `src/cache.ts` (cache state, `getWidget`, two new exports).
- Tests: new `src/cache.test.ts`, run with `bun test` (Bun 1.4.4 is installed; the repository has no package manifest and gains none).
- Callers: none inside the repository; external callers of `getWidget` now receive a shared instance for 30 s, so mutating a returned widget is visible to other callers of the same id within that window.
- Dependencies: none added.

# Spec Delta

## Purpose

Defines how a widget is looked up by id, how long a looked-up widget is reused by later lookups, and how callers invalidate reused widgets.

## ADDED Requirements

### Requirement: Lookup reuses a widget for 30 seconds
A lookup by id SHALL return a widget whose `id` equals the requested id. A lookup of an id whose cached widget was created less than 30 000 ms earlier SHALL return that same widget instance. Lookups of different ids SHALL return different instances.

#### Scenario: Repeated lookup within the TTL
- **WHEN** `getWidget("a")` is called at time T and again at T + 29 999 ms
- **THEN** both calls return the same object instance, and its `id` is `"a"`

#### Scenario: Different ids
- **WHEN** `getWidget("a")` and `getWidget("b")` are called at the same time
- **THEN** they return different instances with `id` `"a"` and `"b"` respectively

#### Scenario: Negative control
- **WHEN** the lookup builds a new widget on every call (no caching)
- **THEN** the check that the second lookup of `"a"` at T + 29 999 ms returns the first call's instance MUST fail

### Requirement: Cached widget expires after 30 seconds
A cached widget SHALL expire 30 000 ms after it was created; a lookup at or after that moment SHALL return a new instance with the same `id` and start a new 30 000 ms lifetime. Lookups SHALL NOT extend a cached widget's lifetime.

#### Scenario: Lookup at the expiry boundary
- **WHEN** `getWidget("a")` is called at time T and again at T + 30 000 ms
- **THEN** the second call returns a different instance whose `id` is `"a"`

#### Scenario: Reads do not extend the lifetime
- **WHEN** `getWidget("a")` is called at T, at T + 20 000 ms, and at T + 30 000 ms
- **THEN** the call at T + 20 000 ms returns the instance from T, and the call at T + 30 000 ms returns a different instance

#### Scenario: New lifetime after expiry
- **WHEN** `getWidget("a")` is called at T, at T + 30 000 ms, and at T + 59 999 ms
- **THEN** the calls at T + 30 000 ms and T + 59 999 ms return the same instance, different from the one at T

#### Scenario: Negative control
- **WHEN** a cached widget never expires, or each lookup restarts its lifetime
- **THEN** the check that the lookup at T + 30 000 ms after reads at T and T + 20 000 ms returns a different instance MUST fail

### Requirement: Invalidating one widget
`invalidateWidget(id)` SHALL remove the cached widget for that id so the next lookup of that id returns a new instance. It SHALL leave other ids' cached widgets in place, and SHALL complete without error for an id that has no cached widget.

#### Scenario: Invalidate a cached id
- **WHEN** `getWidget("a")` and `getWidget("b")` are called, then `invalidateWidget("a")`, then both are looked up again within 30 000 ms of the first calls
- **THEN** the lookup of `"a"` returns a different instance with `id` `"a"`, and the lookup of `"b"` returns the instance from before

#### Scenario: Invalidate an id with no cached widget
- **WHEN** `invalidateWidget("missing")` is called with nothing cached for `"missing"`
- **THEN** the call returns without throwing, and a following `getWidget("missing")` returns a widget with `id` `"missing"`

#### Scenario: Negative control
- **WHEN** `invalidateWidget("a")` leaves the cached widget for `"a"` in place
- **THEN** the check that the next lookup of `"a"` returns a different instance MUST fail

### Requirement: Clearing the widget cache
`clearWidgetCache()` SHALL remove every cached widget, so the next lookup of any previously looked-up id returns a new instance.

#### Scenario: Clear after several lookups
- **WHEN** `getWidget("a")` and `getWidget("b")` are called, then `clearWidgetCache()`, then both are looked up again within 30 000 ms of the first calls
- **THEN** each lookup returns a different instance from before, with the same `id`

#### Scenario: Negative control
- **WHEN** `clearWidgetCache()` removes only some cached widgets, or none
- **THEN** the check that the lookups of both `"a"` and `"b"` after the clear return new instances MUST fail

# Design

## Context

`src/cache.ts:1-3` is the whole module: `getWidget(id)` returns a new `{ id }` literal per call. There is no package manifest, no dependency, no test and no caller elsewhere in the repository. Bun 1.4.4 is installed and runs TypeScript tests directly (`bun test`). Motivation and scope: see proposal.md; required behaviour: see specs/widget-lookup/spec.md.

## Goals / Non-Goals

**Goals:**
- Module-level cache with a fixed 30 000 ms lifetime per entry, measured from creation.
- Memory held by expired entries is released without requiring a lookup of that same id.

**Non-Goals:**
- A size bound or LRU eviction (user decision: TTL only).
- A configurable TTL, per-entry TTLs, or sliding expiry.
- Freezing or copying returned widgets.

## Decisions

### Storage and expiry check
A module-level `Map<string, { widget: { id: string }; createdAt: number }>`. `getWidget(id)` reads `now = Date.now()`, first prunes expired entries (below), then returns the cached widget when `now - createdAt < 30_000`; otherwise it builds `{ id }`, deletes any old entry for the id, inserts the new one, and returns it. `TTL_MS = 30_000` is a module constant. The comparison is strict, so at exactly 30 000 ms the entry is expired (spec: "at or after that moment").

Alternative considered: lazy removal only on a lookup of the same id. Rejected: an id never looked up again would keep its entry forever, an unbounded leak with no size cap.

### Pruning expired entries in insertion order
Every entry has the same TTL and a refreshed entry is deleted before it is re-inserted, so the Map's insertion order is creation order and therefore expiry order. Each `getWidget` call iterates from the front and deletes entries while they are expired, stopping at the first live one. Amortised cost is O(1) per call (each entry is deleted once). No timers, so nothing keeps the process alive and tests need no timer mocking.

### Time source
`Date.now()`. Tests move time with `setSystemTime` from `bun:test`, which changes `Date.now()` (checked on Bun 1.4.4) but not `performance.now()`. A monotonic clock would need a test-only injection point in the public API; see Risks.

### Invalidation
`invalidateWidget(id)` is `Map.delete(id)` (no-op for a missing id); `clearWidgetCache()` is `Map.clear()`. Both are exported from `src/cache.ts`. Tests call `clearWidgetCache()` in `beforeEach` and reset the clock with `setSystemTime()` in `afterEach` so test order does not matter.

### Build vs. adopt: TTL cache
- Repository: none; searched `src/` (only `src/cache.ts:1-3`, no cache), and the repository has no package manifest or installed dependency.
- Platform: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Map provides keyed storage in insertion order but no expiry; https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Date/now provides the clock. No platform TTL cache exists in JavaScript or Bun.
- Candidates:
  - `lru-cache` (https://github.com/isaacs/node-lru-cache): newest release 11.5.3, 2026-09-18 (deps.dev); licence BlueOak-1.0.0; maintained. Supports `ttl` and an injectable `perf.now` clock. # Design

## Context

`src/cache.ts:1-3` is the whole module: `getWidget(id)` returns a new `{ id }` literal per call. There is no package manifest, no dependency, no test and no caller elsewhere in the repository. Bun 1.4.4 is installed and runs TypeScript tests directly (`bun test`). Motivation and scope: see proposal.md; required behaviour: see specs/widget-lookup/spec.md.

## Goals / Non-Goals

**Goals:**
- Module-level cache with a fixed 30 000 ms lifetime per entry, measured from creation.
- Memory held by expired entries is released without requiring a lookup of that same id.

**Non-Goals:**
- A size bound or LRU eviction (user decision: TTL only).
- A configurable TTL, per-entry TTLs, or sliding expiry.
- Freezing or copying returned widgets.

## Decisions

### Storage and expiry check
A module-level `Map<string, { widget: { id: string }; createdAt: number }>`. `getWidget(id)` reads `now = Date.now()`, first prunes expired entries (below), then returns the cached widget when `now - createdAt < 30_000`; otherwise it builds `{ id }`, deletes any old entry for the id, inserts the new one, and returns it. `TTL_MS = 30_000` is a module constant. The comparison is strict, so at exactly 30 000 ms the entry is expired (spec: "at or after that moment").

Alternative considered: lazy removal only on a lookup of the same id. Rejected: an id never looked up again would keep its entry forever, an unbounded leak with no size cap.

### Pruning expired entries in insertion order
Every entry has the same TTL and a refreshed entry is deleted before it is re-inserted, so the Map's insertion order is creation order and therefore expiry order. Each `getWidget` call iterates from the front and deletes entries while they are expired, stopping at the first live one. Amortised cost is O(1) per call (each entry is deleted once). No timers, so nothing keeps the process alive and tests need no timer mocking.

### Time source
`Date.now()`. Tests move time with `setSystemTime` from `bun:test`, which changes `Date.now()` (checked on Bun 1.4.4) but not `performance.now()`. A monotonic clock would need a test-only injection point in the public API; see Risks.

### Invalidation
`invalidateWidget(id)` is `Map.delete(id)` (no-op for a missing id); `clearWidgetCache()` is `Map.clear()`. Both are exported from `src/cache.ts`. Tests call `clearWidgetCache()` in `beforeEach` and reset the clock with `setSystemTime()` in `afterEach` so test order does not matter.

### Build vs. adopt: TTL cache
- Repository: none; searched `src/` (only `src/cache.ts:1-3`, no cache), and the repository has no package manifest or installed dependency.
- Platform: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Map provides keyed storage in insertion order but no expiry; https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Date/now provides the clock. # Gate

- **Mandatory class**: none
- **Depth**: standard (the class is none and no review, gate or release mechanism changes)
- **Risk tier**: product
- **Author's risk assessment**: A wrong expiry comparison or pruning loop would return stale widgets past 30 s or rebuild them too early; a broken invalidation would keep stale widgets after `invalidateWidget`/`clearWidgetCache`. Impact is limited to one in-process module with no callers in the repository, no persistence, no I/O and no trust boundary, so the class is none. The cache is new in-process state, not a changed existing state machine, and JavaScript runs each call to completion, so there is no concurrent access to the Map.
- **Whole-diff review**: not needed (whole-diff surface reviewed in F2)
- **Accepted residual risks**: Wall-clock jumps change entry lifetimes and can delay pruning (design.md, Risks); returned widgets are shared mutable instances for up to 30 s (proposal.md, Impact).
- **Out of scope for blocking**: Size bounds, configurable TTL and freezing returned widgets (design.md, Non-Goals: excluded by user decision).

+A new internal module `src/ttl-store.ts` exports `class TtlStore<K, V>` with `constructor(ttlMs: number, now: () => number)`, `get(key): V | undefined`, `set(key, value): V`, `delete(key): void`, `clear(): void` and a read-only `size`. It holds a `Map<K, { value: V; createdAt: number }>`. `src/cache.ts` creates one module-level `new TtlStore<string, { id: string }>(30_000, () => Date.now())` and implements `getWidget(id)` as `store.get(id) ?? store.set(id, { id })`, `invalidateWidget(id)` as `store.delete(id)` (no-op for a missing id) and `clearWidgetCache()` as `store.clear()`. `src/cache.ts` exports only those three functions; `TtlStore` is not re-exported.
+

# Design

## Context

`src/cache.ts:1-3` is the whole module: `getWidget(id)` returns a new `{ id }` literal per call. There is no package manifest, no dependency, no test and no caller elsewhere in the repository. Bun 1.4.4 is installed and runs TypeScript tests directly (`bun test`). Motivation and scope: see proposal.md; required behaviour: see specs/widget-lookup/spec.md.

## Goals / Non-Goals

**Goals:**
- Module-level cache with a fixed 30 000 ms lifetime per entry, measured from creation.
- Memory held by expired entries is released without requiring a lookup of that same id.

**Non-Goals:**
- A size bound or LRU eviction (user decision: TTL only).
- A configurable TTL, per-entry TTLs, or sliding expiry.
- Freezing or copying returned widgets.

## Decisions

### Storage and expiry check
A module-level `Map<string, { widget: { id: string }; createdAt: number }>`. `getWidget(id)` reads `now = Date.now()`, first prunes expired entries (below), then returns the cached widget when `now - createdAt < 30_000`; otherwise it builds `{ id }`, deletes any old entry for the id, inserts the new one, and returns it. `TTL_MS = 30_000` is a module constant. The comparison is strict, so at exactly 30 000 ms the entry is expired (spec: "at or after that moment").

Alternative considered: lazy removal only on a lookup of the same id. Rejected: an id never looked up again would keep its entry forever, an unbounded leak with no size cap.

### Pruning expired entries in insertion order
Every entry has the same TTL and a refreshed entry is deleted before it is re-inserted, so the Map's insertion order is creation order and therefore expiry order. Each `getWidget` call iterates from the front and deletes entries while they are expired, stopping at the first live one. Amortised cost is O(1) per call (each entry is deleted once). No timers, so nothing keeps the process alive and tests need no timer mocking.

### Time source
`Date.now()`. Tests move time with `setSystemTime` from `bun:test`, which changes `Date.now()` (checked on Bun 1.4.4) but not `performance.now()`. A monotonic clock would need a test-only injection point in the public API; see Risks.

### Invalidation
`invalidateWidget(id)` is `Map.delete(id)` (no-op for a missing id); `clearWidgetCache()` is `Map.clear()`. Both are exported from `src/cache.ts`. Tests call `clearWidgetCache()` in `beforeEach` and reset the clock with `setSystemTime()` in `afterEach` so test order does not matter.

### Build vs. adopt: TTL cache
- Repository: none; searched `src/` (only `src/cache.ts:1-3`, no cache), and the repository has no package manifest or installed dependency.
- Platform: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Map provides keyed storage in insertion order but no expiry; https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Date/now provides the clock. No platform TTL cache exists in JavaScript or Bun.
- Candidates:
  - `lru-cache` (https://github.com/isaacs/node-lru-cache): newest release 11.5.3, 2026-09-18 (deps.dev); licence BlueOak-1.0.0; maintained. Supports `ttl` and an injectable `perf.now` clock. Reject: the required configuration is TTL-only with no `max`, for which its README ("Storage Bounds Safety") says expired items are not purged unless `ttlAutopurge` is set, prints a warning to standard error, and recommends "using a `Map` object" for a cache bound only by TTL.
  - `@isaacs/ttlcache` (https://github.com/isaacs/ttlcache): newest release 2.1.5, 2026-05-21 (deps.dev); licence BlueOak-1.0.0; maintained. Reject: its clock is a fixed `performance.now()` (`src/index.ts:18`) with no injection option, and expiry runs on `setTimeout`; by default `get` still returns an item past its TTL until the timer fires (README, `checkAgeOnGet`), so the 30 000 ms boundary in the spec cannot be tested deterministically without timer mocking.
  - Searches run: web search "npm TTL cache library injectable clock perf option lru-cache ttl"; deps.dev for both packages; both READMEs.
- Decision: build, gap: a TTL-only cache with a deterministic expiry boundary under a test-controlled clock and no new dependency manifest; `lru-cache` advises against its own use for TTL-only caching, and `@isaacs/ttlcache` has no injectable clock and returns stale items until its timer fires.

## Risks / Trade-offs

- [Wall-clock jumps: `Date.now()` moving backwards lengthens entry lifetimes, forwards shortens them] → Accepted; a backwards jump past the creation time gives a negative age and keeps the entry alive until the clock catches up. After a backwards jump, insertion order no longer matches expiry order, so pruning can release some expired entries late; lookups still check each entry's own age, so returned instances stay correct. A monotonic clock would need a test injection point in the public API.
- [Shared mutable instance: a caller mutating a returned widget affects every caller of that id for up to 30 s] → Documented in the proposal's Impact; freezing is a non-goal.
- [Unbounded growth while many distinct ids are looked up within 30 s] → Bounded by the 30 s window; pruning releases them afterwards. No size cap by user decision.

# Proposal

## Why

`getWidget(id)` in `src/cache.ts` builds a new widget object on every call, so callers asking for the same id never share a result. Caching each widget for 30 seconds lets repeated lookups reuse one instance while still picking up a fresh widget after a bounded time, and an explicit invalidation API lets callers drop a stale entry before it expires.

## What Changes

- `getWidget(id)` returns the same widget instance for the same id while that id's cache entry is younger than 30 seconds (30 000 ms).
- An entry expires 30 000 ms after it was created; reads do not extend its lifetime. The first lookup after expiry builds a new widget and starts a new 30-second entry.
- New export `invalidateWidget(id)`: drops that id's entry so the next lookup builds a new widget; other ids are unaffected; an id with no entry is a no-op.
- New export `clearWidgetCache()`: drops every entry.
- The returned widget's shape (`{ id }`) and the `getWidget` signature are unchanged.

Decisions taken with the user before this proposal: time-based expiry (30 s TTL, set after the user's correction from an earlier no-expiry choice), no size bound, and an exported invalidation API.

## Capabilities

### New Capabilities
- `widget-lookup`: looking up a widget by id, including how long a looked-up widget is reused and how callers invalidate it.

### Modified Capabilities

None: the repository has no specs (`openspec list --specs` reports none).

## Impact

- Code: `src/cache.ts` (cache state, `getWidget`, two new exports).
- Tests: new `src/cache.test.ts`, run with `bun test` (Bun 1.4.4 is installed; the repository has no package manifest and gains none).
- Callers: none inside the repository; external callers of `getWidget` now receive a shared instance for 30 s, so mutating a returned widget is visible to other callers of the same id within that window.
- Dependencies: none added.

# Proposal

## Why

`getWidget(id)` in `src/cache.ts` builds a new widget object on every call, so callers asking for the same id never share a result. Caching each widget for 30 seconds lets repeated lookups reuse one instance while still picking up a fresh widget after a bounded time, and an explicit invalidation API lets callers drop a stale entry before it expires.

## What Changes

- `getWidget(id)` returns the same widget instance for the same id while that id's cache entry is younger than 30 seconds (30 000 ms).
- An entry expires 30 000 ms after it was created; reads do not extend its lifetime. The first lookup after expiry builds a new widget and starts a new 30-second entry.
- New export `invalidateWidget(id)`: drops that id's entry so the next lookup builds a new widget; other ids are unaffected; an id with no entry is a no-op.
- New export `clearWidgetCache()`: drops every entry.
- The returned widget's shape (`{ id }`) and the `getWidget` signature are unchanged.

Decisions taken with the user before this proposal: time-based expiry (30 s TTL, set after the user's correction from an earlier no-expiry choice), no size bound, and an exported invalidation API.

- `widget-lookup`: looking up a widget by id, including how long a looked-up widget is reused and how callers invalidate it.

# Design

## Context

`src/cache.ts:1-3` is the whole module: `getWidget(id)` returns a new `{ id }` literal per call. There is no package manifest, no dependency, no test and no caller elsewhere in the repository. Bun 1.4.4 is installed and runs TypeScript tests directly (`bun test`). Motivation and scope: see proposal.md; required behaviour: see specs/widget-lookup/spec.md.

## Goals / Non-Goals

**Goals:**
- Module-level cache with a fixed 30 000 ms lifetime per entry, measured from creation.
- Memory held by expired entries is released without requiring a lookup of that same id.

**Non-Goals:**
- A size bound or LRU eviction (user decision: TTL only).
- A configurable TTL, per-entry TTLs, or sliding expiry.
- Freezing or copying returned widgets.

## Decisions

### Internal TTL store, separate from the public module
A new internal module `src/ttl-store.ts` exports `class TtlStore<K, V>` with `constructor(ttlMs: number, now: () => number)`, `get(key): V | undefined`, `set(key, value): V`, `delete(key): void`, `clear(): void` and a read-only `size`. It holds a `Map<K, { value: V; createdAt: number }>`. `src/cache.ts` creates one module-level `new TtlStore<string, { id: string }>(30_000, () => Date.now())` and implements `getWidget(id)` as `store.get(id) ?? store.set(id, { id })`, `invalidateWidget(id)` as `store.delete(id)` (no-op for a missing id) and `clearWidgetCache()` as `store.clear()`. `src/cache.ts` exports only those three functions; `TtlStore` is not re-exported.

Why a separate module: pruning (below) is not observable through the public API, and the injected `now` lets its tests drive time directly. Spec behaviour is tested through `src/cache.ts`; pruning and `size` through `src/ttl-store.ts`.

Alternative considered: a Map inside `src/cache.ts` plus an exported size accessor. Rejected: it adds a public export the user did not ask for, only to make an internal property testable.

### Expiry check
`get(key)` reads `t = now()`, prunes (below), then returns the entry's value when `t - createdAt < ttlMs`; otherwise it deletes the entry and returns `undefined`. `set(key, value)` deletes any existing entry for the key, inserts `{ value, createdAt: now() }` and returns `value`. The comparison is strict, so at exactly 30 000 ms the entry is expired (spec: "at or after that moment"). Reads never update `createdAt`.

Alternative considered: lazy removal only on a lookup of the same id. Rejected: an id never looked up again would keep its entry forever, an unbounded leak with no size cap.

### Pruning expired entries in insertion order
Every entry has the same TTL and `set` deletes before it re-inserts, so the Map's insertion order is creation order and therefore expiry order. Each `get` iterates from the front and deletes entries while `t - createdAt >= ttlMs`, stopping at the first live one. Amortised cost is O(1) per call (each entry is deleted once). No timers, so nothing keeps the process alive and tests need no timer mocking.

### Time source
`src/cache.ts` passes `() => Date.now()`, read on every call so `setSystemTime` from `bun:test` moves it (checked on Bun 1.4.4: `setSystemTime` changes `Date.now()` but not `performance.now()`). `src/cache.test.ts` calls `clearWidgetCache()` in `beforeEach` and resets the clock with `setSystemTime()` in `afterEach`, so test order does not matter. `src/ttl-store.test.ts` injects a mutable counter as `now`.

### Build vs. adopt: TTL cache
- Repository: none; searched `src/` (only `src/cache.ts:1-3`, no cache), and the repository has no package manifest or installed dependency.
- Platform: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Map provides keyed storage in insertion order but no expiry; https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Date/now provides the clock. No platform TTL cache exists in JavaScript or Bun.
- Candidates:
  - `lru-cache` (https://github.com/isaacs/node-lru-cache): newest release 11.5.3, 2026-09-18 (deps.dev); licence BlueOak-1.0.0; maintained. Supports `ttl` and an injectable `perf.now` clock. Reject: the required configuration is TTL-only with no `max`, for which its README ("Storage Bounds Safety") says expired items are not purged unless `ttlAutopurge` is set, prints a warning to standard error, and recommends "using a `Map` object" for a cache bound only by TTL.
  - `@isaacs/ttlcache` (https://github.com/isaacs/ttlcache): newest release 2.1.5, 2026-05-21 (deps.dev); licence BlueOak-1.0.0; maintained. Reject: its clock is a fixed `performance.now()` (`src/index.ts:18`) with no injection option, and expiry runs on `setTimeout`; by default `get` still returns an item past its TTL until the timer fires (README, `checkAgeOnGet`), so the 30 000 ms boundary in the spec cannot be tested deterministically without timer mocking.
  - Searches run: web search "npm TTL cache library injectable clock perf option lru-cache ttl"; deps.dev for both packages; both READMEs.
- Decision: build, gap: a TTL-only cache with a deterministic expiry boundary under a test-controlled clock and no new dependency manifest; `lru-cache` advises against its own use for TTL-only caching, and `@isaacs/ttlcache` has no injectable clock and returns stale items until its timer fires.

## Risks / Trade-offs

- [Wall-clock jumps: `Date.now()` moving backwards lengthens entry lifetimes, forwards shortens them] → Accepted; a backwards jump past the creation time gives a negative age and keeps the entry alive until the clock catches up. After a backwards jump, insertion order no longer matches expiry order, so pruning can release some expired entries late; lookups still check each entry's own age, so returned instances stay correct. A monotonic clock would need a test injection point in the public API.
- [Shared mutable instance: a caller mutating a returned widget affects every caller of that id for up to 30 s] → Documented in the proposal's Impact; freezing is a non-goal.
- [Unbounded growth while many distinct ids are looked up within 30 s] → Bounded by the 30 s window; pruning releases them afterwards. No size cap by user decision.

# Delegation and Parallel Dispatch (omp)

**Pick the agent by reasoning difficulty, not diff size.** `scout`/`sonic` run on the cheap
`@smol` model: give them only lookups and mechanical edits. A one-line change that needs an
evidence document cross-checked, a serialization format preserved, or git history reasoned
about goes to `task` (or stays with you). `oracle` is for architecture calls and debugging
after two failed attempts; `auditor`/`reviewer` are for finished diffs; `plan-reviewer` for plans and fix deltas.

**Overlapping tasks never run in the same batch.** Derive each item's file-set from the plan's
`Files:` lines or the scope. Items overlap when their sets intersect, including shared barrels,
i18n, tokens, and config. Overlapping items go in separate `task` calls, one after the other;
disjoint items may share a batch. An unknown file-set overlaps everything.
Items that are read-only reviewers over the same committed inputs (the `review-work` gate lanes, the `omp-gated` plan-review scopes) do not overlap and may share a batch; editing items keep this rule.

**Two or more concurrent editing tasks run isolated.** Pass `isolated: true` on the task item
(or enable `task.isolation.enabled`), so each child edits its own APFS clone and its changes
come back as a patch. A real collision then surfaces as a failed apply, not a silent interleave.

**A running subagent owns its files.** Do not edit them until its result arrives (`wait`, or the
delivered `task-result`). A staged-but-uncommitted tree looks the same as finished work.

**Reviews stay small and start fresh.** Split a large review by shared files into 2-3 reviewer
tasks, not one per angle. Put the `file:line` inventory and only the relevant plan excerpt in the
brief; ask for blockers with `file:line`, at most 5 notes, and one verdict line. A re-review
after fixes is a new task with the delta and the open blockers, never a follow-up message to the
old reviewer (`write agent://...`). The review-work TRAILER REPAIR. message is not a re-review: it
goes to the same reviewer by design. A procedure that prescribes its own brief overrides this
paragraph: review-work and integration-review dispatch their verbatim briefs, and the OpenSpec
`omp-gated` review artifact dispatches its fixed brief for every round, with the two paths filled
in and nothing added.

**After every editing subagent:** check `git reflog <default-branch> -3` and `git worktree list`.
Unexpected movement of the default branch is an incident to report.
